Suppose we want to find the inverse of the matrix 

$$
A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{array} \right]}.
$$ 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
$$
[{\color{blue}{A}}\, |\, {\color{black}I_2}]	
=	
\left[{\begin{array}{cc|cc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}7} & 0 & 1\end{array}}\right]
$$

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}7} & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & 0 & {\color{red}7} & {\color{red}-2} \\ 0 & 1 & {\color{red}-3} & {\color{red}1}\end{array}\right] \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
A^{-1} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}7 & - 2 \\ - 3 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can easily check our result by computing $AA^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the eigenvalues of a $3\times 3$ matrix in much the same way as for $2\!\times\! 2$ matrices. 

Remember, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ for some non-zero vector $\mathbf{v}$. This implies that the equation

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has a non-trivial solution, which means that the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, and consequently
$\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0.$
Therefore, if we want to find the eigenvalues of a $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A,$ we have to find the solutions of the characteristic equation

$$
\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

Let's go through this process in the case of the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}- 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & - 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{array} \right]}.
$$

First, we write down the matrix $A-\lambda I{:}$

﻿﻿﻿

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -8-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set and solve the characteristic equation $\,\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0.$ Using the fact that the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the elements on the main diagonal, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -8-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )(5-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +8)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda=-2,$ $\lambda=-8,$ and $\lambda=5.$

The **algebraic multiplicity** of an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the number of times it is a solution of the characteristic equation. 

For example, consider a $6\times 6$ matrix $A$ with the following characteristic equation:

$$
(\lambda-{\color{red}4})(\lambda-{\color{red}4})(\lambda-1)(\lambda+8)^{\color{blue}3} =0
$$

The eigenvalue $\lambda={\color{red}4}$ is a double root. Therefore, it has algebraic multiplicity $2.$ 

By the same reasoning, we say that 

- $\lambda=1$ has algebraic multiplicity $1,$ and

- $\lambda=-8$ has algebraic multiplicity $\color{blue}3$.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\color{red}{a}_{11}}x+{\color{red}{a}_{12}}y & ={\color{blue}{b}_{1}} \\ {\color{red}{a}_{21}}x+{\color{red}{a}_{22}}y & ={\color{blue}{b}_{2}},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and let
$$
A = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}{a}_{11}} & {\color{red}{a}_{12}} \\ {\color{red}{a}_{21}} & {\color{red}{a}_{22}}\end{array} \right]},
\quad
\mathbf{x} = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]},
\quad
\mathbf{b} =
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}{b}_{1}} \\ {\color{blue}{b}_{2}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Recall that we can write the system as $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ The **invertible matrix theorem** says the following statements are equivalent:

1\. $A$ is invertible (that is, $A^{-1}$ exists).

2\. The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for any $2 \times 1$ column vector $\mathbf{b}$ (we call such systems consistent independent).

\displaystyle \mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

5\. The  determinant of $A$ is nonzero (that is, $\det(A) \neq 0$).
